title: Why binary search needs so few steps
subject: algorithm

brief.audience: programmers meeting the algorithm for the first time

scenes.why: Opening: a surprising number, then the promise to explain it.

beats.say: Finding one value in a sorted list of a million items takes at most twenty comparisons.
Here is how eleven lines of Python manage that.

scenes.why: The claim is that halving needs far fewer looks than scanning. Running both on the same list, with a count, shows it.
scenes.heading: two ways to find 57

beats.say: The obvious way to search is to check every item in turn. Finding 57 here takes six looks.
Binary search checks the middle, throws half the list away, and gets there in two.

scenes.why: The loop is the algorithm: show each line next to what it does to the search range.
scenes.heading: binary_search.py · one search, line by line

beats.say: Start with two markers, lo and hi, at the two ends of the sorted list.
Each time around the loop, look at the middle item.
23 is less than 57, so everything from the middle down is ruled out, and lo jumps past it.
Second pass. The middle is now 57, which is the target, so we return its index.

scenes.why: The speed claim is a formula; show the halving that produces it.
scenes.heading: why it is fast

beats.say: Every pass throws away half of what is left.
So a list of n items needs about log base two of n passes. For a million items, that is twenty.

scenes.why: Recap: the precondition, the mechanism, the cost.
scenes.title: What to remember

items.text: The list must already be sorted
About log₂ n passes: twenty for a million items

beats.say: Three things to remember. The list has to be sorted first.
And that is why a million items take only about twenty passes.
